lead: North Dakota's cold winters and wide-open prairie shape its fire risk. SootMend helps homes and businesses from Fargo to Bismarck recover from fire, smoke and soot.
risk: heating fires in long winters, wind-driven prairie fires, and kitchen fires
risk_short: heating fires, prairie fires, house fires
why: North Dakota winters are among the coldest in the lower 48. Furnaces, propane heaters and space heaters run for months, and about 14% of homes use propane. A fire that knocks out heat can freeze pipes within hours, adding water damage.

Prairie fires can move fast in wind. In 2024, FEMA approved a major disaster declaration for North Dakota wildfires and straight-line winds. Rural homes and farms often rely on volunteer fire departments with long response distances.
problems: Homes in Fargo, Bismarck, Grand Forks and Minot
Frozen pipes after a winter fire
Smoke odor in homes and shops
tips: Service furnaces and propane heaters every fall.
Keep a fire extinguisher in the shop and the kitchen.
Mow firebreaks around farm buildings before fall.
If a fire cuts the heat in winter, protect the plumbing right away.
insurance: Farm and ranch policies cover the house, shops and equipment under separate limits, so check each one after big purchases.
areas: Fargo, Bismarck, Grand Forks, Minot, West Fargo, Williston and rural counties are all covered.

faq.q: How fast do pipes freeze after a winter fire?
faq.a: In North Dakota cold, pipes in an unheated house can freeze within hours. After a fire, have the water shut off or the lines drained, or set up temporary heat as soon as it is safe.
